result.summary: The Argo sails through the Hellespont to the Doliones, where a night battle by mistake kills their king Cyzicus, and the heroes appease Rhea on Dindymum. At the Mysian coast Heracles loses Hylas to a nymph, and the Argonauts sail on without him, reconciled after Glaucus explains the fates.

scenes.title: Departure and Hellespont Passage
scenes.summary: The heroes row off, stop at Electra's island for rites by Orpheus' order, and pass through the Hellespont.
scenes.stakes: The dangers of the sea voyage, which the rites are meant to make safer.

scenes.title: Welcome by King Cyzicus
scenes.summary: The Argo reaches the Doliones' land, protected from the Earthborn, and Cyzicus hosts the heroes in friendship.

scenes.title: Battle with the Earthborn
scenes.summary: The Earthborn block the harbour, but Heracles and the heroes slay them all, and the Argo sails.
scenes.stakes: The ship trapped in the harbour by six-armed monsters.

scenes.title: Night Battle and Cyzicus' Death
scenes.summary: Contrary winds return the Argo by night; the Doliones mistake them for enemies, and Jason kills Cyzicus. Grief, funeral, and Cleite's suicide follow.
scenes.stakes: Cyzicus faces his fated death; the Doliones face ruin and grief.

scenes.title: Propitiating the Mountain Mother
scenes.summary: Storms hold the Argo; Mopsus interprets a halcyon's cry, and the heroes sacrifice to Rhea on Dindymum, and the winds cease.

scenes.title: Rowing Contest and Heracles' Oar
scenes.summary: The heroes race at the oars; Heracles breaks his oar, and at Cius the Mysians welcome them. He goes to cut a pine for a new oar.

scenes.title: Hylas Taken by the Nymph
scenes.summary: Hylas is drawn into the spring by a nymph; Polyphemus hears his cry and tells Heracles, who rages in search.
scenes.stakes: Hylas is seized and drowned; Heracles loses his beloved companion.

scenes.title: Left Behind: Glaucus' Prophecy
scenes.summary: The Argo sails without Heracles; Telamon quarrels, Glaucus reveals the fates, and Jason and Telamon reconcile.
scenes.stakes: The crew's unity and the voyage after losing its greatest hero.

scenes.title: Landing on a Beach
scenes.summary: After a night of wind then calm, the heroes row to a broad beach at sunrise.

place.name: Beach on a bend of the coast

notable_quotes.reason: Poet's reflection that no mortal escapes fate.
Glaucus reveals Hylas' fate as husband of a nymph.
Vivid bull-and-gadfly simile for Heracles' frantic grief.

analysis.text: Fate and error: Cyzicus dies by a tragic mistake despite friendly hospitality, and Glaucus shows that Heracles' separation is divinely ordained.
The episode explains cult practices and place names around Cyzicus and Cius, such as the hero worship, the common mill, Rhea's drum rites and Hylas search ritual.

legacy.text: The Hylas abduction by water nymphs became a favourite subject in art, notably John William Waterhouse's painting Hylas and the Nymphs (1896).

fun_facts.text: Apollonius, a scholar-poet at Alexandria, used local cult explanations (aitia) like those here to link myth to real places.

language_notes.text: "Spake" is archaic for "spoke"; the speaker is Jason, ending his address to the crew.
The rites "that may not be uttered" are the mystery rites of Samothrace (Electra's island), secret initiation believed to protect sailors.
"The maiden daughter of Athamas" is Helle, who fell from the golden ram and drowned, giving the Hellespont its name.
"The Far-Darter" is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god, here as giver of oracles.
Cyzicus had been told by a prophecy to welcome a band of heroes peacefully rather than fight them.
"As with Jason" compares Cyzicus to Jason: both are young, with beards just beginning to grow.
Dindymum is a mountain near Cyzicus, used as a lookout; the poet explains a local place name, "path of Jason."
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose"; the narrator offers a personal opinion.
The "strong bolts" are the ship's timbers or ribs; logs are soaked in seawater, probably to season them for shipbuilding.
The Sacred Rock is an aetiology: the poet explains a local place name from this event, as he does with the fountain Cleite.
"Pelasgian" is a vague old term for early Greek peoples; the Doliones take the Argonauts for hostile Macrians in the dark.
"Son of Oeneus" is Meleager; "the two sons of Tyndareus" (sentence 38) are Castor and Polydeuces.
"Minyan" is a name for the Argonauts, many of whom descended from the Minyans of Iolcus.
The "cornmill" refers to grinding grain for bread; eating food "untouched by fire" shows they did no cooking in mourning.
Halcyon is the kingfisher, a sea bird fabled to calm the winds and waves. Its cry here serves as a prophetic omen.
Propitiate means to appease a deity by offering prayers and sacrifice so as to win her favour.
'Are complete' means the elements are fulfilled or ordered through her power. She is presented as the foundation of the whole cosmos.
Titias and Cyllenus are Idaean Dactyls, mythical divine attendants of the Mother. Here they are called 'dispensers of doom' and her assessors, sharing in her judgments.
The ill-omened cry is the lament of the Doliones for their king Cyzicus, whom the Argonauts had accidentally killed. The noise drowns it out.
This explains a Phrygian cult custom: the wheel (a spinning instrument or tambourine-like object) and drum were used in worship of Rhea.
'I ween' is archaic for 'I think' or 'I suppose', a narrator's aside.
Poseidon's storm-footed steeds are the sea god's immortal horses, who draw his chariot over the waves; the phrase says the Argo outran even them.
"Forspent" is archaic for utterly exhausted.
A cairn is a mound of stones, here a monument marking the tomb or memorial of Aegaeon.
A delver is a digger, a laborer who works the soil with a spade.
Apollo Ecbasius means Apollo of Disembarkation, a title for sacrifices made when landing after a sea voyage.
Heracles is the son of Zeus (the translation's spelling here), whom Zeus fathered with the mortal Alcmena.
Orion's setting in late autumn was associated with storms at sea, so sailors feared it; hence "baleful."
"Nurture" means he raised and trained Hylas as his attendant; "carried him off" means taken after Theiodamas was killed.
"Smitten with the curse" means Theiodamas was struck by a doom or ill fate, here Heracles' violent demand.
Pegae means "springs" in Greek; the name belongs to a place on the Propontis coast in Mysia, where the Argonauts have landed.
Cypris is Aphrodite, goddess of love, named for Cyprus. Her power makes the nymph fall in love.
"Recks not" means pays no heed; "cheek" here means a check or restraint on his running.
The Posideian headland is a promontory near Cius, named for Poseidon; the Argo is leaving the Mysian coast where Heracles and Hylas were lost.
"If so be that" means "if it happens that"; Telamon bitterly accuses Jason of leaving Heracles so that Heracles' fame would not outshine his own.
The games over Pelias dead are the funeral games for Pelias, the king who sent Jason on the quest. The Boreads were killed on Tenos afterward.
Glaucus was a mortal fisherman turned into a sea-god; he is here called interpreter of Nereus, the old sea-god known for truthful prophecy.
Heracles' twelve toils were set by Eurystheus of Argos; after them he became immortal and lived among the gods.
"Were fain" means "would gladly wish"; Jason says he would like Telamon to defend him likewise.
"He" is Heracles, whose threat comes from the later story; the sentence jumps back to events after the departure, with "doom" meaning fate.

context_notes.text: The six-armed Earthborn giants are local monsters, born from the earth; they will later attack the Argonauts.
Poseidon, god of the sea, was the ancestor of the Doliones, so he shielded them from the giants.
Apollo "Ecbasian" is invoked as god of disembarking; the epithet comes from ekbasis, landing.
Heracles was left to guard the ship with younger heroes while the others climbed the mountain.
Hera persecuted Heracles throughout his life because he was Zeus's son by another woman.
Aeson's son is Jason, leader of the Argonauts. He kills Cyzicus, the Doliones' king, who had earlier welcomed them kindly.
Funeral games and circling the tomb in armour were traditional heroic honours for the dead, as for Patroclus in the Iliad.
Mopsus is a seer, a prophet who interprets omens from birds. Acastus is the son of Pelias, who joined the voyage.
Rhea is the Mother of the gods and mother of Zeus, linked with Phrygian mountain-worship as the Mountain Mother (Cybele).
Argus is the shipbuilder of the Argo. Here he carves the goddess's rough wooden cult image from an old vine stump.
The Argonautica often explains local names and rites by a story of the heroes' visit; here the spring of Jason is credited to this event.
Heracles is the strongest of the Argonauts. His breaking the oar prepares the episode in which he is left behind in Mysia.
The bow, quiver, lion's skin and club are Heracles' signature gear; the lion's skin comes from the Nemean lion he killed.
Hylas was Heracles' young companion and squire, and the Argonauts' stop in Mysia leads to Heracles' separation from the voyage.
Artemis was goddess of wild places and the hunt, and nymphs of mountains and woods were her attendants.
Polyphemus, an Argonaut, is a companion of Heracles here; he is not the Cyclops of the Odyssey.
Tiphys is the Argo's helmsman, who reads winds and weather and decides when the ship should sail.
Telamon, son of Aeacus, is a powerful hero and later father of the great Ajax.
The sons of Thracian Boreas, Zetes and Calais, are winged heroes, children of the North Wind.
Polyphemus, a Argonaut here, was left in Mysia and founded Cius; this Polyphemus is not the Cyclops.

literary_notes.text: The poet speaks in the first person, refusing to reveal the sacred mysteries and presenting himself as a pious singer.
The giants' extra arms and fierce nature give a vivid, monstrous picture and prepare for danger later.
Leaving his bride and bed to host strangers shows Cyzicus as generous and trusting.
The slain giants are compared to felled logs laid on the beach, turning the grim scene into a vivid image of labour.
Battle spreading like fire in dry brushwood conveys how quickly and destructively the confusion grows.
The narrator announces the king's doom before the blow, creating tragic inevitability.
Fate as a wide snare or net surrounding all mortals expresses the inescapability of death.
The fleeing Doliones are likened to doves before hawks, stressing their helplessness against the heroes.
Friends and hosts have killed each other by mistake, a tragic irony revealed only at dawn.
The bird's prophecy of calming winds foreshadows the later end of the storm and shows divine concern for the voyage.
Fruit, flowers and gentle beasts paint a picture of nature responding with abundance, showing the goddess's favour.
Wild beasts fawn on the men like dogs, as if the natural world itself welcomed the sacrifice.
The brisk closing summary moves from feast to dawn and departure, resolving the episode and returning the story to the voyage.
The extended comparison to a weary laborer going home at evening compares Heracles' idle, tired hands and the heroes' hunger and landing to a homely scene.
Uprooting a deep-rooted pine with its clods of earth, by hand, conveys Heracles' superhuman strength.
The pine's uprooting is likened to a gust tearing a mast from a ship, giving a sense of sudden violent force.
The poet interrupts himself to address the audience, showing his control over how much backstory his song includes.
Sound and touch bring the abduction vividly to life: the ringing bronze, the nymph's arms, the sudden plunge.
Polyphemus is compared to a hungry beast hearing sheep it cannot reach, conveying his frustrated, futile search.
Sweat pouring and blood boiling exaggerate Heracles' physical reaction to show overwhelming grief and alarm.
The extended bull-and-gadfly comparison shows Heracles' maddened, directionless frenzy, alternating between rushing and stopping to shout.
"Eating out his heart" pictures Jason's grief as something consuming him from within, showing his silent helplessness as leader.
Telamon's sparkling eyes are likened to ravening flame, conveying his violent rage.
The narrator anticipates the Boreads' later death at Heracles' hands, adding a note of doom to the quarrel.
The restless wave "wraps" Glaucus and the water foams and dashes, giving the sea a lively, almost purposeful motion as the god departs.
